title: The Gaussian Is Enough: Flow-Matching Priors Do Not Help When Fine-Tuning Large Behavior Models

paper.title: The Gaussian Is Enough: Flow-Matching Priors Do Not Help When Fine-Tuning Large Behavior Models Thanks: Correspondence to: chen.xu@tri.global
paper.abstract: Abstract Modern robot imitation learning increasingly relies on generative policies based on diffusion or flow-matching models, which generate actions by transforming samples from a prior distribution. A key question is whether the choice of prior matters. Replacing the standard Gaussian with a closer-to-target, non-Gaussian prior has been shown to substantially improve performance when training from scratch . A natural next step is to ask whether these gains transfer to fine-tuning pretrained Large Behavior Models (LBMs) such as LBM 1.0, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and GR00T N1.5, where one might expect even larger gains. Surprisingly, we find that this is not the case, except possibly at very low fine-tuning data fractions. Across over 100K simulation rollouts spanning all three aforementioned LBMs on 40+ tasks in two simulation platforms, and 1250 hardware rollouts on five bimanual manipulation tasks, non-Gaussian priors that are demonstrably closer to the target yield statistically indistinguishable or worse fine-tuning performance than a standard Gaussian prior. Diagnostic analyses suggest why: fine-tuned imitation learning policies converge to similar action predictions across priors, despite their fine-tuned encoder embeddings diverging substantially from the pretrained embeddings and each other. A learning-rate ablation further confirms that encoder training is the dominant factor in fine-tuning performance, substantially outweighing the effect of prior choice. We conclude with concrete directions for future research on when and why learned priors might still matter in fine-tuning. Project page: https://cxu-tri.github.io/non_gaussian_FT/ .

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Imitation learning for robot manipulation increasingly employs generative models, such as diffusion and flow-matching policies [ 1 , 2 ] , which transport samples from a prior distribution p 0 p_{0} to a target action distribution conditioned on observations. Large Behavior Models (LBMs) scale this approach: pretrain once on diverse vision, language, and robot action data, then fine-tune on a modest set of task-specific demonstrations. Recent examples include LBM 1.0 [ 3 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 4 ] , and GR00T N1.5 [ 5 ] . By default, these LBMs use an isotropic Gaussian 𝒵 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) as the prior, though flow matching [ 6 ] is agnostic to p 0 p_{0} by construction. In other words, the Gaussian is a convention, not a requirement. A line of recent work [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] has exploited this flexibility when training from scratch : learning single-task policies without loading weights pretrained on large-scale data. Replacing the Gaussian with a closer-to-target prior substantially improves success rates on common benchmarks such as LIBERO [ 11 ] , MetaWorld [ 12 ] , and Adroit [ 13 ] . It remains unknown whether this benefit carries over to fine-tuning pretrained LBMs, where policies are initialized from pretrained weights rather than learned from scratch. A natural question arises: Can we fine-tune more capable policies by starting from an informed action prior rather than a standard Gaussian? Swapping the Gaussian for another distribution, such as actions sampled from the pretrained LBM itself, requires no change to the training pipeline. The intuition is appealing: if the prior is already close to the target, the policy only needs to traverse a short transport distance in action space, and doing so should facilitate fine-tuning and improve policy performance ( Fig. 1 ). a 0 ∼ 𝒵 a_{0}\sim\mathcal{Z} (Gaussian) a 0 ∼ A pre a_{0}\sim A_{\text{pre}} (pretrained prior) Fig. 1: Prior definition and visualization. The Gaussian 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} (left) produces incoherent, random motion, while A pre A_{\text{pre}} (right) already makes partial task progress by picking up the avocado and moving it to the bin, reflecting a prior close to the target action. We hypothesize that the close-to-target prior A pre A_{\text{pre}} would outperform 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} after policy fine-tuning, but we empirically find that this is not the case. We therefore evaluate whether the from-scratch-training benefits of non-Gaussian priors persist after LBM pretraining. If so, learned priors would compound the gains from pretraining with no change to the deployment pipeline. Surprisingly, we consistently obtain negative results to this question based on average success rates and average task progress across tasks ( Fig. 2 ). The priors that help when training from scratch almost always do not improve fine-tuning performance, and in several regimes they do worse than the default Gaussian prior. The full comparison across all seven prior variants ( Fig. 3 ) confirms that most priors we consider yield statistically indistinguishable performance after fine-tuning, and, thus, provide no benefit to the policy. To our knowledge, this paper is the first large-scale study of non-Gaussian action priors for LBM fine-tuning. We make three contributions: • A negative finding at scale: Non-Gaussian priors that are demonstrably closer to the target yield fine-tuning performance that is statistically indistinguishable from, or worse than, a standard Gaussian. This holds both on average and for the majority of individual tasks. • Consistency across the fine-tuning design space: The finding is consistent across seven prior constructions, most data fractions (25%–100% of fine-tuning data), three LBM architectures (LBM 1.0, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and GR00T N1.5), as well as both simulation and robot hardware settings. One exception is the very-low-data regime (5% fraction), which we discuss in Section VIII . • An introspective explanation: Across priors, three diagnostics reveal that fine-tuned encoder embeddings diverge from pretrained embeddings and each other, yet yield indistinguishable conditional action likelihoods, and the resulting policy head outputs comparable action predictions. A learning-rate ablation confirms that encoder training matters far more than prior choice for policy performance, pointing to the pretrained encoder, not the prior, as the dominant factor. In short, action priors shape fine-tuning training dynamics, particularly in the observation embedding space, but do not affect policy performance.

sections.heading: II-A Flow-Matching and Diffusion Policies for Robotics
sections.text: Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become prominent approaches for visuomotor imitation learning. At their core, both families define time-dependent transport between a prior and target distribution in action space. Single-task diffusion policy [ 1 ] introduced the formulation, which was then extended in BESO [ 2 ] to goal-conditioned settings, and scaled in LBMs [ 14 , 4 , 3 , 5 ] . Compared to DDPM-based diffusion models [ 15 ] , flow-matching variants [ 6 ] take a more direct path from the prior to the target distribution and make no distributional assumption on the prior. These desirable properties are central to recent flow policies [ 5 , 4 ] and to this paper. Within the generative policy paradigm, LBMs (e.g., LBM 1.0 [ 3 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 4 ] , and GR00T N1.5 [ 5 ] ) pretrain on large-scale, diverse manipulation data before fine-tuning on downstream tasks, but by default use the Gaussian prior distribution in both pretraining and fine-tuning. Parallel empirical studies of fine-tuning design choices (action-space parameterization [ 16 ] , data scaling [ 17 ] , co-training [ 18 ] ) have examined many axes of the recipe but hold the prior fixed. Our paper investigates the effect of action prior choice on policy fine-tuning performance.

sections.heading: II-B Pretraining, Transfer Learning, and Introspection
sections.text: Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model’s learned representations to new tasks, a form of transfer learning that has proven highly effective. Prior works have shown that pretrained features improve performance in both computer vision [ 19 , 20 ] and robotics: frozen pretrained encoders [ 21 , 22 ] , shared trunks [ 23 ] , and full pretrained policies [ 3 , 5 , 4 ] all outperform training from scratch. Other works examine what explains whether a pretrained model transfers well to a new task. Training-free probes such as LogME [ 24 ] estimate the predictive power of pretrained features. Scaling-law studies [ 25 , 26 ] and likelihood-based assessments [ 27 ] examine when pretraining metrics can be trusted as proxies for downstream policy performance. Our work applies these introspective tools to the choice of prior: we compare priors using downstream performance ( Section VI ) and training-free metrics, such as LogME, per-observation ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance, and cosine similarity in action and embedding spaces ( Section VII ).

sections.heading: II-C Non-Gaussian Prior Distributions
sections.text: A growing body of work has proposed structured non-Gaussian priors for policy learning. BRIDGER [ 8 ] trains a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) to produce informative action priors. Cocos [ 9 ] uses a condition-dependent Gaussian whose parameters are learned from observations to prevent loss collapse. Retrieval [ 39 , 40 , 41 ] constructs the action prior from nearest-neighbor actions, with distances measured in the observation embedding space. Action-to-action flow matching [ 7 ] maps demonstration actions directly to target actions for single-step inference. Other variants include equivariance guarantees for non-Gaussian priors [ 10 ] , cluster-based and residual-action priors [ 28 , 29 ] , and Schrödinger-bridge formulations [ 30 , 31 ] . In each case, however, the proposed prior is evaluated by training a policy from scratch; none of these works investigates whether the benefit transfers to fine-tuning a pretrained LBM. A complementary line of research modifies the prior without changing the policy’s weights. Frozen-policy steering methods operate on the latent noise space of a trained policy: DSRL [ 32 ] defines a reward function over the noise space to denoise high-reward noise samples, Golden Ticket [ 33 ] searches for optimal constant noise vectors, and GoldenStart [ 34 ] trains a Q-guided CVAE noise prior. Related inference-time warm-starting methods [ 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 ] adjust the prior at rollout time. These methods change sampling, not training, and apply to any pretrained policy. Since we focus on the effects of training-time priors in fine-tuned policies, these approaches are outside the scope of this work.

sections.heading: III Problem Setup
sections.text: Setting. We fine-tune a pretrained LBM π pre \pi_{\text{pre}} on task-specific demonstration datasets and consider whether replacing the default Gaussian prior with a non-Gaussian prior improves the fine-tuned policy performance. The pretrained policy π pre \pi_{\text{pre}} can be any flow-matching- or diffusion-based LBM (in our experiments: LBM 1.0 [ 3 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 4 ] , or GR00T N1.5 [ 5 ] ). Notation. We follow the diffusion policy notation [ 1 ] . The target a 1 a_{1} is an action chunk ( H H steps of future actions) drawn from the demonstration dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . The raw observation o o (camera images, language instructions, proprioception) is passed through the LBM’s vision-language-action encoder to produce the observation embedding e e , which conditions the action-head network v θ v_{\theta} . The action head is trained to transport prior samples a 0 ∼ p 0 a_{0}\sim p_{0} to targets a 1 a_{1} . We write a 0 ∼ p 0 a_{0}\sim p_{0} for a generic prior sample; the specific prior constructions (e.g., 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} , A pre A_{\text{pre}} , etc.) defined in Section IV each instantiate p 0 p_{0} . We use “prior” throughout the paper to refer to p 0 p_{0} . Why flow matching is the right testbed. Flow matching (FM) [ 6 ] regresses a velocity field directly between prior and target samples. The conditional FM objective ℒ FM \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}} = 𝔼 t , a 0 , a 1 ​ ‖ v θ ​ ( a t , t ∣ e ) − ( a 1 − a 0 ) ‖ 2 , \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t,a_{0},a_{1}}\left\|v_{\theta}(a_{t},t\mid e)-(a_{1}-a_{0})\right\|^{2}, (1) a t \displaystyle a_{t} = ( 1 − t ) ​ a 0 + t ​ a 1 , \displaystyle=(1-t)\,a_{0}+t\,a_{1}, only requires paired samples ( a 0 , a 1 ) (a_{0},a_{1}) from the prior and target, so swapping p 0 p_{0} from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) to any other distribution requires no change to the training or inference procedure. DDPM-style diffusion models [ 15 ] , by contrast, are designed around a forward noising process whose stationary distribution is Gaussian. Replacing this distribution would require redesigning the noise schedule, objective, and sampling procedure, which are non-trivial changes.

We include three representative external priors effective for policy learning. • Cocos [ 9 ] is a condition-dependent Gaussian whose mean is produced by passing the observation embedding e e through a small encoder into the action space. The encoder is jointly trained with a decoder that maps back to the embedding space of e e . • BRIDGER [ 8 ] is a CVAE-based action prior that maps a Gaussian latent to an action chunk, conditioned on the observation embedding e e . • Retrieval ( k k -NN) [ 39 , 40 , 41 ] is a non-parametric prior that averages the k k nearest-neighbor action chunks from a frozen bank indexed by the observation embedding e e . The three cited works used k k -NN actions directly as policies; we repurpose this approach as a prior for fine-tuning. Some existing non-Gaussian prior methods, such as action-to-action FM [ 7 ] and VITA [ 42 ] , replace the policy network with a custom architecture, conflating the effect of the prior with architectural changes. These methods are thus incompatible with fine-tuning from pretrained weights. The seven priors above all preserve the pretrained encoder and action-head weights, so only the prior differs across experiments .

sections.heading: V Experimental Setup
sections.text: In this section, we detail our experimental setup for evaluating whether and under what conditions non-Gaussian priors benefit policy fine-tuning. We cover: how we control for confounds, test for statistical significance, evaluate in simulation and on robot hardware, and define our plotting conventions.

sections.heading: V-A Experimental Controls
sections.text: Throughout the paper, we hold the task, data, architecture, optimizer, and number of fine-tuning steps identical across all prior variants within each experimental setting (see Appendix C for hyperparameter choices). This protocol applies uniformly to all settings. For prior noise levels, we select σ A \sigma_{A} and σ E \sigma_{E} via grid search ( Fig. 19 ; values in Appendix A ).

sections.heading: V-B Statistical Testing
sections.text: We treat policy comparison as a formal hypothesis test rather than only reporting empirical average success rates, following prior work [ 3 , 18 , 43 ] . For binary success/failure we use the STEP statistical framework [ 43 ] ; for continuous metrics (per-observation ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance and cosine similarity) we use Welch’s t t -test [ 44 ] . All tests use a global significance level α = 0.05 \alpha{=}0.05 (95% confidence level). When more than two priors are compared we apply Bonferroni correction: the family-wise false-positive probability of m m independent pairwise tests at level α \alpha is 1 − ( 1 − α ) m 1-(1-\alpha)^{m} . Bonferroni controls this by testing each pair at α / m \alpha/m such that the overall false-positive rate is upper-bounded by α \alpha . A compact letter display (CLD) [ 45 ] concisely summarizes each method comparison: two methods share at least one alphabetical letter if and only if their pairwise difference is not significant at the corrected level. Implementation details (STEP’s anytime-valid guarantee, Lai’s [ 46 ] fallback at per-method sample sizes above ∼ 600 {\sim}600 , and CLD ordering conventions) are in Appendix B .

sections.heading: V-C Hardware A/B testing
sections.text: Following best practices for robot policy evaluation [ 47 ] , hardware rollouts use blind A/B testing: for each fixed initial condition (IC), all priors under evaluation are run in a randomized order before moving to the next IC, ensuring the human operator does not know which prior is being tested at any given trial. This design eliminates operator bias and, because priors are interleaved rather than grouped by prior, distributes any ambient drift (e.g., lighting, wear, operator attention) approximately equally across all priors.

sections.heading: V-D Benchmarks
sections.text: We use two simulators and one hardware setup. The LBM Eval [ 3 ] Drake-based [ 48 ] simulation benchmark serves as our main testbed. It consists of eight bimanual manipulation tasks of varying difficulty and sample sizes (approximately 196–392 per task at 100%) that were unseen during the pretraining phase for LBM 1.0 (see [ 3 ] for pretraining data selection). We also evaluate on the RoboCasa365 [ 49 ] MuJoCo-based [ 50 ] simulation suite. This benchmark is split into 18 atomic tasks (single-step manipulations, e.g., opening a cabinet) and 16 composite tasks (multi-step sequences, e.g., preparing coffee), totaling 34 tasks. Hardware is a tabletop bimanual setup with two Franka FR3 arms and parallel grippers. Each rollout is scored by a human with a binary success label and a task-specific partial task progress rubric. The latter decomposes the task into ordered milestone predicates (e.g., rotor picked up , rotor seated , lockring tightened ) and reports the fraction of milestones achieved. Hardware details and per-task demonstration counts are in Appendix C .

sections.heading: V-E Plotting Conventions
sections.text: In all figures, an ( ↑ \uparrow ) arrow indicates higher is better and a ( ↓ \downarrow ) arrow lower is better. Violin plots for binary success rates show Bayesian posterior distributions; a black horizontal tick marks the posterior mean and a colored dot marks the empirical mean. Violin plots for continuous metrics (e.g., ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance, cosine similarity, task progress) show empirical distributions with a colored dot at the empirical mean. All plots are annotated with CLD letters: methods sharing a letter are statistically indistinguishable; methods with different letters are statistically separable. sections.heading: VI Research Questions and Results
sections.text: Our experiments are guided by three research questions: (Q1) Do non-Gaussian priors that are measurably closer to the target improve policy fine-tuning performance? (Q2) Do informed priors have an advantage across data fractions, particularly in the low-data regime where the added inductive bias may be most beneficial? (Q3) Is the effect of prior choice consistent across model architectures as well as simulation and hardware experiments? We design four experimental settings, summarized in Table II , to carefully study these three questions. Setting A isolates Q1 using a contrived prior that is by construction closer in ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance to the target action distribution than the Gaussian. Setting B sim addresses both Q1 and Q2 by varying the amount of fine-tuning data across five fractions on eight tasks. Setting B real tests Q3 on whether the result transfers to hardware. Setting C further studies Q3 on other LBMs by repeating the experiments on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.5. We consistently find that non-Gaussian priors do not improve fine-tuning, with a possible exception in very low-data regimes. Alongside each main setting we run targeted ablations (encoder learning rate, training objective, noise scale), each isolating a single confounding variable.

sections.heading: VI-A Setting A: Fraction-Pretrained Prior
sections.text: The key challenge in studying non-Gaussian priors for fine-tuning is controlling prior quality: a pretrained LBM has never seen the fine-tuning task, so its zero-shot actions may be out-of-distribution and form a weak prior. A null result would then be hard to tell apart from a poor-quality prior. Setting A therefore isolates this question by constructing an artificially strong prior that is measurably close to the target in ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance. We use a two-stage pipeline: first, the pretrained LBM 1.0 is fine-tuned using the Gaussian prior on 50% of the demonstrations to produce a task-aware checkpoint whose actions are much closer to the target than the Gaussian ( Fig. 2 , left); second, this checkpoint serves as the “pretrained model” for another round of fine-tuning, in which we vary only the prior. We evaluate on five kitchen-scenario tasks from LBM Eval (see Table VI for full names) and compare all seven priors from Table I , with 200 rollouts per task (1000 total per prior). Results. Fig. 3 summarizes the key finding across all seven prior variants. When training from scratch (i.e., training the same LBM 1.0 architecture from random weight initialization), all non-Gaussian priors (except for Cocos; see Appendix A ) outperform the Gaussian baseline 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} based on empirical success rates, though they are largely statistically indistinguishable. The simplest of our proposed priors, A pre A_{\text{pre}} , significantly outperforms 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} (CLD “a” vs. “bc”) with an average success rate of roughly 28% vs. 18%. This is consistent with prior work on non-Gaussian priors in the from-scratch regime [ 8 , 9 , 7 ] . Nevertheless, this empirical advantage disappears entirely in the fine-tuning regime: A pre A_{\text{pre}} becomes the worst-performing method based on success rate and no prior is statistically separable from the Gaussian. Additionally, the posterior distributions overlap more substantially in the fine-tuning case than in the from-scratch case, reflecting the lesser impact of action priors on policy performance during fine-tuning. sections.heading: VI-B Setting B sim {}_{\text{sim}} : LBM Fine-Tuning in Simulation
sections.text: Setting A tests Q1 and finds no prior advantage under a controlled good prior at small scale. Two questions remain for the practical fine-tuning regime. First, do priors matter at full LBM scale without the artificial construction in Setting A (Q1)? Second, how do learned priors perform across fine-tuning data fractions, especially in the low-data regime that may benefit from inductive biases of learned priors (Q2)? To address both questions, we fine-tune the LBM 1.0 model on the eight LBM Eval unseen tasks and sweep over multiple data fractions (5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of available demonstrations). This mirrors the standard LBM deployment pipeline [ 3 , 18 ] . Of the eight tasks, three are comparatively easier (higher success rates under the standard Gaussian) and five are harder; we report both the overall average and the per-task breakdown ( Appendix D ). Each of the seven priors is evaluated with 200 rollouts per prior–task–fraction combination, totaling 56,000 simulation rollouts for this setting. Results. Fig. 4 shows the success rates averaged across the eight simulation tasks as a function of data fraction. At every data fraction from 25% upward, most prior variants cluster closely and all share the CLD letter “a”. The one exception is at 5% data, where E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} outperforms 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} (CLD “a” vs. “bc,” 25.9% vs. 18.9% success rate). Intuitively, at such a low data fraction the demonstrations cover only a small portion of the target action space, and the embedding-space jitter from E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} appears to act as an informative inductive bias that the Gaussian cannot provide. This very low-data regime (approximately 10–20 demonstrations per task) is the one exception in our study where a learned prior helps. All priors are statistically indistinguishable or worse than 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} across fractions. The one exception is E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} at 5% data, which significantly outperforms 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} .

sections.heading: VI-C Setting B real {}_{\text{real}} : LBM Fine-Tuning on Robot Hardware
sections.text: Settings A and B sim both rely on simulation, which could in principle mask simulation-specific artifacts. The hardware setting tests whether the finding holds under real-world conditions that cannot be replicated in simulation. We fine-tune LBM 1.0 on five bimanual FR3 hardware tasks, spanning varying difficulty levels: FoodBank , ClearKitchenCounter [ 3 ] , GatheringIngredientsForCookies , BusBin , and BikeRotorInstall [ 3 ] . Per-task descriptions and demonstration counts are in Appendix C . We compare five of the seven prior variants: 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} (the standard Gaussian baseline), E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} , Cocos, BRIDGER 1 1 1 Its CVAE training was unstable on both simulation and hardware datasets (NaN losses, requiring restarts with different random seeds until stable); despite this instability, stable runs of BRIDGER were included in the evaluation. , and Retrieval, with 50 A/B-test rollouts per prior per task (250 per prior, 1250 total; protocol in Section V ). The remaining two priors, A pre A_{\text{pre}} and A pre + σ A ​ 𝒵 A_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{A}\mathcal{Z} , were dropped after a pilot study ( Section D-F ) in which all three action-space priors were statistically tied and E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} was selected as the representative learned prior for the full evaluation. Results. Fig. 5 shows full results across the five bimanual FR3 hardware tasks. Out of 250 A/B-test rollouts per prior, four of the five priors (i.e., 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} , E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} , Cocos, and Retrieval) fall in the same CLD group “a,” with partial-progress scores in the 71–77% range. BRIDGER is the sole outlier (group “b,” partial progress ∼ 56 % {\sim}56\% ), consistent with the training instability noted earlier and documented in Appendix A . Excluding BRIDGER, the pattern mirrors our simulation findings: the choice of prior has no statistically significant effect on fine-tuning performance. sections.heading: VI-D Setting C: Validation on Other LBM Architectures
sections.text: Settings A, B sim , and B real all use LBM 1.0 as the backbone, which uses a CLIP encoder and DiT action head. Setting C tests whether the results generalize across model architectures and simulation environments. We repeat the comparison on the RoboCasa simulation benchmark using two additional LBMs: π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 4 ] (fused SigLIP + Gemma 2B with interleaved cross-attention) and GR00T N1.5 [ 5 ] (Eagle-2 VLM + diffusion transformer action expert). Each model is fine-tuned on each of the 34 RoboCasa tasks and evaluated with 200 rollouts per task (see Section D-H for per-task breakdowns). The fused architecture constrains which priors can be ported from the LBM 1.0 experiments. Of the seven priors from Setting B sim , four have natural analogues here: 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} (Gaussian), A pre A_{\text{pre}} (pretrained actions), A pre + σ A ​ 𝒵 A_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{A}\mathcal{Z} (action + noise), and Retrieval ( k k -NN in the LBM’s vision-encoder feature space, k = 3 k{=}3 ). We construct A pre A_{\text{pre}} for each model from a frozen copy of itself (e.g., π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s A pre A_{\text{pre}} uses frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ). The embedding-space priors E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} , Cocos, and BRIDGER are not immediately portable because both LBMs lack a single bottleneck embedding: visual and action tokens are fused across many transformer layers with per-layer cross-attention, leaving no natural injection point. They are thus omitted in this setting. Results. Fig. 6 reports success rates for atomic and composite tasks separately for each of the two LBMs. Both architectures exhibit the same qualitative ordering across task types: 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} and A pre + σ A ​ 𝒵 A_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{A}\mathcal{Z} tie at the top in CLD group “a,” while the pure learned prior A pre A_{\text{pre}} falls into group “b”; Retrieval is either “b” or in a distinct group “c.” Despite the observed performance degradation of A pre A_{\text{pre}} and Retrieval, A pre A_{\text{pre}} remains ∼ 3 × {\sim}3\times closer to the target than 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} in ℓ 2 \ell_{2} on RoboCasa ( Fig. 21 ), the same factor as in Setting A on LBM Eval ( Fig. 2 , left). Yet A pre A_{\text{pre}} degrades only here in Setting C, indicating that geometric proximity to the target is not what drives the gap. A key difference in this setting compared to the earlier ones is that LBM 1.0’s pretraining includes simulation data from the same simulator, whereas π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.5 were pretrained predominantly on real-world data. This domain gap specifically hurts A pre A_{\text{pre}} and Retrieval because both rely solely on a frozen copy of the pretrained LBM (for action generation and for building the retrieval bank, respectively). We hypothesize that the other two priors, 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} and A pre + σ A ​ 𝒵 A_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{A}\mathcal{Z} , are regularized by random noise and thus are less affected by this domain gap. sections.heading: VII Analysis: Why Does the Prior Not Matter Under Fine-Tuning?
sections.text: Summarizing the negative-result experiments against our research questions, we found that Q1 (closer priors should help) yields a negative answer, Q2 (advantage across fine-tuning data fractions) is only partly supported at 5% data, and Q3 (generalization across policies and hardware) also yields a negative answer. The experimental results thus raise a central question: if a non-Gaussian prior is measurably closer to the target distribution (in Setting A by construction, and in Settings B and C empirically), why does this proximity not translate to better fine-tuning performance? We approach this question from two complementary perspectives. First, we ask whether fine-tuned models converge toward the target despite starting from different priors. We examine convergence at two levels: whether different priors produce encoder features with comparable predictive power for the target actions ( Section VII-A ), and whether the resulting action predictions are similarly close to ground truth ( Section VII-B ). Second, we ask whether fine-tuned models diverge from a shared starting point : that is, whether different priors lead to structurally different optimization trajectories, as measured by ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance and cosine similarity in the action or embedding space ( Section VII-C ). The observed embedding-space divergence motivates a natural hypothesis: fine-tuning performance is governed primarily by the observation encoder rather than by the prior itself. We test this hypothesis directly through a learning-rate ablation that deliberately undertrains the encoder ( Section VII-D ). All analyses in this section are carried out in Setting B sim (LBM 1.0 simulation), where we have the most comprehensive results: seven prior variants × \times five data fractions × \times eight tasks, enabling controlled comparisons across the prior–data landscape. We focus on four representative priors: 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} (Gaussian), A pre A_{\text{pre}} (pure learned prior, closest to target), A pre + σ A ​ 𝒵 A_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{A}\mathcal{Z} (action + noise; defined in Section IV ), and E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} (embedding + noise). The baselines (Cocos, BRIDGER, Retrieval) are omitted from these introspective ablations as their performance was found to be worse than or comparable to these four priors. Action-space metrics are computed on the flattened action chunk. Embedding-space metrics are computed on the observation embedding e e defined in Section III . For notation, we reuse A pre A_{\text{pre}} from Section IV (actions drawn from the frozen pretrained policy) and introduce A post A_{\text{post}} for the corresponding actions drawn from the fine-tuned policy. The observation embedding e e ( Section III ) has two instances depending on the encoder checkpoint: E pre = e π pre ​ ( o ) E_{\text{pre}}=e_{\pi_{\text{pre}}}(o) is the embedding from the pretrained encoder, and E post = e π post ​ ( o ) E_{\text{post}}=e_{\pi_{\text{post}}}(o) is the embedding from the fine-tuned encoder, evaluated on the same o o .

sections.heading: VII-A Feature Quality: LogME Analysis
sections.text: We begin at the feature layer, asking whether fine-tuned observation encoders produce features of equal predictive power for the target actions, regardless of the prior used during training. We measure this with LogME [ 24 ] , a training-free proxy for feature quality that estimates the log marginal evidence of a Bayesian linear regression from encoder features E post E_{\text{post}} to ground-truth actions A target A_{\text{target}} . LogME produces a single aggregate score per prior–task–fraction combination by fitting a weight matrix to all (observation-embedding, action) pairs. Higher LogME indicates more predictive encoder features for action prediction. As shown in Fig. 7 , LogME scores are inseparable across all priors. The prior thus governs how much the encoder restructures, but not the quality of the final result: all priors arrive at features that are equally predictive of actions ( Section VII-A ). Fig. 7: LogME feature quality as percentage difference from 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} at each fraction (Setting B sim , eight tasks). A value of five means LogME for that prior is 5% higher than 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} (dashed green line at zero) at the same fraction. Ribbons show ± 1 \pm 1 standard error across the eight tasks. We normalize because raw LogME drops sharply from 5% to 25% data due to a small-sample artifact of the LogME computation (see raw values in Fig. 13 ); normalizing to 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} removes this artifact since we only compare across priors at the same sample size. CLD letters (computed on raw values) confirm all priors share group “a” at every fraction.

sections.heading: VII-B Action-Space Similarity After Fine-Tuning
sections.text: Section VII-A established convergence at the feature layer: fine-tuned observation encoders are equally predictive of actions across priors. We now examine convergence at the output layer, asking whether the post-fine-tuning predicted actions A post A_{\text{post}} converge to the ground-truth actions A target A_{\text{target}} in the target demonstration data. Quantitatively, we measure the per-observation ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance (computed over random samples in the demonstration data; Fig. 8 ) and the per-observation cosine similarity ( Fig. 8 ). The two metrics probe complementary aspects of the action discrepancy: ℓ 2 \ell_{2} captures both magnitude and directional errors, while cosine similarity is scale-invariant and isolates directional agreement. We also note that the per-prior sample size in these distributions is very large ( n ≈ 16000 n{\approx}16000 per prior per fraction), so Welch’s t t -test with Bonferroni correction can detect extremely small mean differences. CLD letters here should therefore be interpreted as indicators of any detectable mean difference, not as indicators of practically significant separation. The post-fine-tuning action predictions are broadly similar across priors under both metrics, with violin distributions that overlap substantially at every fraction. Under ℓ 2 \ell_{2} ( Fig. 8 ), the Gaussian prior ( 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} ) consistently shows a slightly higher (worse) mean distance ( ∼ 6.4 {\sim}6.4 ) than the non-Gaussian priors ( ∼ 5.7 {\sim}5.7 – 5.9 5.9 ), with the absolute gap remaining below 0.8 at every data fraction. Under cosine similarity ( Fig. 8 ), the four priors still have largely overlapping violins, with means within ∼ 0.79 {\sim}0.79 – 0.83 0.83 at every fraction; again, 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} is consistently slightly worse (lower cosine similarity). Note that this small open-loop gap in both metrics does not translate into closed-loop success rate differences ( Fig. 4 , except against E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} at 5%), suggesting it is within the noise tolerance of the downstream rollout evaluation. These action-space results confirm that post-fine-tuning predictions are similar across priors, consistent with the equal feature quality reported in Section VII-A . Violins show per-observation distances between predicted and ground-truth actions at each fraction, with CLD letters from Welch’s t t -test. Top: ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance ( ↓ \downarrow ). All four priors cluster within a narrow range (5.7–6.4), with the Gaussian consistently ∼ 0.5 {\sim}0.5 higher than the non-Gaussian priors. Bottom: cosine similarity ( ↑ \uparrow ). sections.heading: VII-C Representation Divergence Despite Similar Outputs
sections.text: The preceding two analyses together characterize convergence toward the target : fine-tuned observation encoders produce features of indistinguishable quality for action prediction ( Section VII-A ), and their action predictions reach the ground truth with broadly comparable accuracy ( Section VII-B ). We now shift perspective and measure divergence from the pretrained starting point : how much do the model’s representations change during fine-tuning, and does the amount of change depend on the prior? If different priors induce different amounts of change, this would indicate that prior choices affect the optimization landscape yet admit multiple equally good solutions as judged by closed-loop performance. We quantify this also at two levels (action-space and embedding-space) using two complementary metrics: the per-observation ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance between pre- and post-fine-tuning outputs ( Fig. 9 ) and the corresponding per-observation cosine similarity ( Fig. 10 ). Note that absolute ℓ 2 \ell_{2} values are not directly comparable across the two panels because the action and embedding spaces have different dimensionalities; cosine similarity is scale-free and enables direct comparison. Action-space change. Across all priors, the post-fine-tuning actions remain close to their pretrained counterparts: both ℓ 2 \ell_{2} metrics ( ∼ \sim 2.5–2.9) and cosine similarity metrics ( ∼ \sim 0.92–0.95) span a narrow band (top figures of Fig. 9 and Fig. 10 ). The takeaway is that fine-tuning makes comparable adjustments to the action output across priors, though A pre A_{\text{pre}} shifts slightly less (smaller ℓ 2 \ell_{2} metrics and higher cosine similarity) from the pretrained starting point than the other priors. Embedding-space change. In the observation embedding space ( E post E_{\text{post}} vs. E pre E_{\text{pre}} ), however, the priors diverge sharply, and the CLD analysis reveals statistically significant separation at every data fraction under both ℓ 2 \ell_{2} ( Fig. 9 bottom) and cosine similarity ( Fig. 10 bottom). The Gaussian prior shows the smallest change (CLD group “a”), meaning the encoder barely moves from its pretrained state. The learned prior A pre A_{\text{pre}} , however, induces the largest restructuring (group “d”), roughly 2 to 2.5 times the Gaussian’s ℓ 2 \ell_{2} change and the largest drop in cosine similarity. The mixed priors A pre + σ A ​ 𝒵 A_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{A}\mathcal{Z} and E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} fall between these extremes, each occupying a distinct CLD group under both metrics. Practical significance. The action-space distributions ( Fig. 9 top) also show statistically distinct CLD groups, but their empirical distributions overlap almost entirely—the detected differences are too small to be practically meaningful. In contrast, the embedding-space separability corresponds to large, visually apparent gaps between the violin distributions, particularly at lower data fractions, and the same prior ranking holds under both ℓ 2 \ell_{2} and cosine metrics. We speculate one possible explanation for the large embedding-space changes: because the Gaussian was used during pretraining, fine-tuning with 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} only shifts the target action distribution toward the fine-tuning task data while the prior remains unchanged. Fine-tuning with a pretrained action prior A pre A_{\text{pre}} , in contrast, shifts both the prior and the target relative to the pretrained policy, forcing the encoder to compensate more. Mixed priors that combine noise with pretrained actions dilute this shift and produce intermediate encoder changes. Fig. 9: How much does fine-tuning change the model’s internal representations? The prior thus governs how much the encoder restructures, but not the quality of the final result: all priors arrive at features that are equally predictive of actions ( Section VII-A ). This view resonates with previous loss landscape analyses [ 19 , 20 ] on vision transfer learning, where different encoder configurations could lead to equivalent downstream performance. In our case, it is likely that the prior determines which local minimum the optimizer settles into, but these local minima are comparably effective downstream. Whether this divergence in encoder representations has other implications for transfer learning, beyond the downstream success rate we measure here, remains to be explored.

sections.heading: VII-D Encoder Training Matters More Than Prior Choice
sections.text: The previous subsection shows that with respect to the pretrained policy, action-space changes after fine-tuning are relatively small (significant overlap in the violins), whereas the observation encoder restructures substantially across priors. This naturally raises the question: how much does encoder training quality matter relative to prior choice? If the encoder dominates and the prior is secondary, then degrading the encoder should hurt performance far more than changing the prior. We test this by reducing the observation encoder’s learning rate to 1 / 10 1/10 of the action head’s, deliberately undertraining it while keeping all other hyperparameters identical. In simulation, we run this ablation on the LBM 1.0 model with three representative priors— 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} (Gaussian baseline), E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} (best-performing among our proposed priors), and Cocos (most recent external baseline)—across all eight Setting B sim tasks at 100% data ( Fig. 11 ). Reducing the encoder learning rate consistently and significantly degrades performance across all three priors: success rates drop from the 56–59% range to the 41–43% range. Statistical tests confirm significant degradation for all three priors (reduced-LR variants share CLD group “b”; standard-LR variants share group “a”). Moreover, the magnitude of degradation is comparable across priors, which is exactly the expected result if the encoder, not the prior, is the dominant factor. Fig. 11: Encoder learning rate ablation. Top: Setting B sim B_{\mathrm{sim}} (eight tasks, 100% data, three representative priors). Reducing the encoder LR to 1 / 10 1/10 of the action head’s (lighter violins, “b”) degrades performance by 15–17% across all three priors, while the choice of prior has minimal effect within each LR group (both groups share a single CLD letter). Bottom: Setting B real (Gaussian prior, five tasks). Reducing the encoder LR to 1 / 10 1/10 drops both success rate and partial task progress (different CLD groups), a larger effect than any prior-related difference in this study. On hardware (Setting B real ), we validate this finding with the Gaussian prior across five tasks ( Fig. 11 ). The standard encoder LR achieves 37% success rate, while the reduced 1 / 10 1/10 LR drops to 28%, a statistically significant decrease (different CLD letters). This hardware result confirms the simulation finding: undertraining the encoder has a far larger impact on policy quality than any prior-related change we study. Overall, observation-encoder training quality is the dominant factor in fine-tuning performance: within each encoder-LR regime, the choice of action-space prior makes no measurable difference, while changing the encoder’s learning rate shifts performance by an amount that exceeds any prior-related effect. This resonates with recent work on run-time monitoring [ 51 , 52 ] , which found that policy encoder embeddings carry rich information predictive of downstream task success. Our encoder-LR ablation supports the view that the quality of these embeddings is a critical lever for policy performance.

sections.heading: VIII-A Implications for Practitioners
sections.text: In practice, the standard Gaussian prior is sufficient for fine-tuning LBMs with a flow-matching action head. Implementing learned priors adds engineering complexity with no measurable benefit. Our encoder-LR ablation ( Section VII-D ) suggests that the key factor appears to be not the prior itself but the quality of the pretrained representations: once the encoder is sufficiently well-pretrained, the encoder dominates the transport regardless of where the flow starts. On the other hand, in the from-scratch regime without pretrained models, learned priors may still be valuable, improving success rates even though differences could be statistically indistinguishable, as supported by both our results and prior work [ 8 , 9 , 7 , 10 ] .

sections.heading: VIII-B Limitations
sections.text: Our findings are established on three LBMs (LBM 1.0, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and GR00T N1.5). The prior-independence finding holds consistently across all three, suggesting it is not an artifact of a particular model capacity or architecture. Nevertheless, we cannot rule out that much larger or smaller models, or models trained on special pretraining distributions, might behave differently. Similarly, our fine-tuning datasets are relatively small (20–400 demonstrations per task); whether the prior-independence finding persists under substantially larger or more diverse fine-tuning data remains open. Our proposed explanation, that the pretrained encoder dominates the action prior choices, is plausible at other scales but remains unverified. Although the metrics we use (LogME, per-observation ℓ 2 \ell_{2} , and cosine similarity) are widely adopted in the transfer learning literature [ 24 , 19 ] , alternative metrics such as LEEP [ 53 ] or H-Score [ 54 ] could reveal additional aspects of how priors affect LBM fine-tuning that we have not explored.

sections.heading: VIII-C Future Work
sections.text: We point out three concrete research directions: 1. Where is the transition? At 5% data in Setting B sim (approximately 20 demonstrations per task), E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} shows significant improvements over 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} . This hints at a regime where the prior begins to matter, but the boundary is not clearly characterized. Mapping this transition as a function of dataset size, task complexity, and model capacity would let practitioners decide when learned priors are worth the engineering cost. 2. Why do different priors yield divergent encoder representations of equal quality? Our analysis shows that they do, but not why the loss landscape admits multiple equally good encoder configurations. Loss-landscape geometry, plasticity [ 55 ] , and linear mode connectivity [ 56 ] are all plausible directions worth investigating. 3. Does encoder divergence have downstream consequences? Different priors lead to structurally different encoders with indistinguishable nominal policy performance. Whether these solutions differ in robustness to distribution shift, continual-learning stability, or catastrophic forgetting is an open question with practical implications.

sections.heading: IX Conclusion
sections.text: We presented a large-scale empirical study of non-Gaussian priors under LBM fine-tuning for visuomotor imitation learning. Across 100K+ cross-architecture simulation rollouts on 40+ tasks in two simulation platforms, and 1250 hardware rollouts, the evidence consistently points in the same direction: learned priors that help when training from scratch do not improve fine-tuning performance. Diagnostic analyses reveal that regardless of prior choice, fine-tuned encoders yield indistinguishable conditional action likelihoods, and the resulting policy outputs similar actions. However, their encoder representations diverge from the pretrained model and each other. An encoder-LR ablation further confirms that the observation encoder, not the prior, is the dominant factor. These findings corroborate that the standard Gaussian prior used in current LBM fine-tuning pipelines is a well-supported choice. More broadly, given these negative results, we hope to inspire the community to explore the underlying learning dynamics of large-scale visuomotor architectures, focusing on why certain components (such as the observation encoder) matter more than others and how that understanding can improve different aspects of downstream robot policy performance.

sections.heading: Appendix B Statistical Testing Details
sections.text: This appendix expands on the condensed stats description in Section V . STEP for binary outcomes. Sequential Testing for Efficient Policy Comparison (STEP) [ 43 ] provides strict error control with adaptive stopping for success/failure comparisons. Because STEP’s false-positive rate is guaranteed to stay below a specific value (e.g., 0.05) at any stopping time (“anytime-valid” error control), we can monitor the test as rollouts accumulate and stop as soon as the result is decisive, without inflating the false-positive rate. Lai fallback at large n n . At per-method sample sizes above ∼ 600 {\sim}600 , STEP’s per-comparison computation becomes heavy; we fall back to the Lai sequential test [ 46 ] , which is near-optimal asymptotically for the same hypothesis class. The fallback is used for the per-task CLD plots in Section D-H where n n accumulates across tasks. Welch’s t t -test for continuous outcomes. For continuous metrics (per-observation ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance and cosine similarity in Section VII ) we use Welch’s t t -test [ 44 ] . The per-method sample sizes in our experiments (typically ≥ 10000 {\geq}10000 ) allow tight central-limit-theorem approximation for the sample mean. Compact letter display (CLD) [ 45 ] . CLD assigns one or more letters to each method such that two methods share at least one letter if and only if their pairwise difference is not significant at the corrected level. Letters are typically ordered by mean performance (earlier letters = better) unless false negatives occur between some pairs. For example, a four-method CLD of “a,” “ab,” “b,” “c” means the first and third differ significantly, the second is indistinguishable from the first and third, and the fourth is strictly worse than all others.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.27070v1 [cs.RO] 22 Sep 2026 The Gaussian Is Enough: Flow-Matching Priors Do Not Help When Fine-Tuning Large Behavior Models Thanks: Correspondence to: chen.xu@tri.global Chen Xu Affiliation: Toyota Research Institute Rishi Shah Affiliation: Woven by Toyota Hadas Kress-Gazit Affiliation: Cornell University Haruki Nishimura Affiliation: Toyota Research Institute and Masha Itkina Affiliation: Toyota Research Institute Abstract Modern robot imitation learning increasingly relies on generative policies based on diffusion or flow-matching models, which generate actions by transforming samples from a prior distribution. A key question is whether the choice of prior matters. Replacing the standard Gaussian with a closer-to-target, non-Gaussian prior has been shown to substantially improve performance when training from scratch . A natural next step is to ask whether these gains transfer to fine-tuning pretrained Large Behavior Models (LBMs) such as LBM 1.0, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and GR00T N1.5, where one might expect even larger gains. Surprisingly, we find that this is not the case, except possibly at very low fine-tuning data fractions. Across over 100K simulation rollouts spanning all three aforementioned LBMs on 40+ tasks in two simulation platforms, and 1250 hardware rollouts on five bimanual manipulation tasks, non-Gaussian priors that are demonstrably closer to the target yield statistically indistinguishable or worse fine-tuning performance than a standard Gaussian prior. Diagnostic analyses suggest why: fine-tuned imitation learning policies converge to similar action predictions across priors, despite their fine-tuned encoder embeddings diverging substantially from the pretrained embeddings and each other. A learning-rate ablation further confirms that encoder training is the dominant factor in fine-tuning performance, substantially outweighing the effect of prior choice. We conclude with concrete directions for future research on when and why learned priors might still matter in fine-tuning. Project page: https://cxu-tri.github.io/non_gaussian_FT/ . Index Terms: Imitation learning, flow-matching & diffusion policies, action priors, large behavior models, fine-tuning. I Introduction Imitation learning for robot manipulation increasingly employs generative models, such as diffusion and flow-matching policies [ 1 , 2 ] , which transport samples from a prior distribution p 0 p_{0} to a target action distribution conditioned on observations. Large Behavior Models (LBMs) scale this approach: pretrain once on diverse vision, language, and robot action data, then fine-tune on a modest set of task-specific demonstrations. Recent examples include LBM 1.0 [ 3 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 4 ] , and GR00T N1.5 [ 5 ] . By default, these LBMs use an isotropic Gaussian 𝒵 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) as the prior, though flow matching [ 6 ] is agnostic to p 0 p_{0} by construction. In other words, the Gaussian is a convention, not a requirement. A line of recent work [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] has exploited this flexibility when training from scratch : learning single-task policies without loading weights pretrained on large-scale data. Replacing the Gaussian with a closer-to-target prior substantially improves success rates on common benchmarks such as LIBERO [ 11 ] , MetaWorld [ 12 ] , and Adroit [ 13 ] . It remains unknown whether this benefit carries over to fine-tuning pretrained LBMs, where policies are initialized from pretrained weights rather than learned from scratch. A natural question arises: Can we fine-tune more capable policies by starting from an informed action prior rather than a standard Gaussian? Swapping the Gaussian for another distribution, such as actions sampled from the pretrained LBM itself, requires no change to the training pipeline. The intuition is appealing: if the prior is already close to the target, the policy only needs to traverse a short transport distance in action space, and doing so should facilitate fine-tuning and improve policy performance ( Fig. 1 ). a 0 ∼ 𝒵 a_{0}\sim\mathcal{Z} (Gaussian) a 0 ∼ A pre a_{0}\sim A_{\text{pre}} (pretrained prior) Fig. 1: Prior definition and visualization. Bottom: schematic of an example flow-matching policy. The action head v θ v_{\theta} is conditioned on the encoder embedding e e and takes in diffusion step t t as well as the action prior p 0 p_{0} . Only the prior varies across our experiments. Top: samples drawn directly from two examples of the prior p 0 p_{0} on the simulated DumpVegetablesIntoContainer task from LBM Eval [ 3 ] , with overlaid colored dots showing both arms’ predicted end-effector positions over the action chunk horizon. Color gradient indicates temporal ordering within the chunk, with lighter dots representing predictions further into the future. The Gaussian 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} (left) produces incoherent, random motion, while A pre A_{\text{pre}} (right) already makes partial task progress by picking up the avocado and moving it to the bin, reflecting a prior close to the target action. We hypothesize that the close-to-target prior A pre A_{\text{pre}} would outperform 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} after policy fine-tuning, but we empirically find that this is not the case. We therefore evaluate whether the from-scratch-training benefits of non-Gaussian priors persist after LBM pretraining. If so, learned priors would compound the gains from pretraining with no change to the deployment pipeline. Surprisingly, we consistently obtain negative results to this question based on average success rates and average task progress across tasks ( Fig. 2 ). The priors that help when training from scratch almost always do not improve fine-tuning performance, and in several regimes they do worse than the default Gaussian prior. The full comparison across all seven prior variants ( Fig. 3 ) confirms that most priors we consider yield statistically indistinguishable performance after fine-tuning, and, thus, provide no benefit to the policy. To our knowledge, this paper is the first large-scale study of non-Gaussian action priors for LBM fine-tuning. We make three contributions: • A negative finding at scale: Non-Gaussian priors that are demonstrably closer to the target yield fine-tuning performance that is statistically indistinguishable from, or worse than, a standard Gaussian. This holds both on average and for the majority of individual tasks. • Consistency across the fine-tuning design space: The finding is consistent across seven prior constructions, most data fractions (25%–100% of fine-tuning data), three LBM architectures (LBM 1.0, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and GR00T N1.5), as well as both simulation and robot hardware settings. One exception is the very-low-data regime (5% fraction), which we discuss in Section VIII . • An introspective explanation: Across priors, three diagnostics reveal that fine-tuned encoder embeddings diverge from pretrained embeddings and each other, yet yield indistinguishable conditional action likelihoods, and the resulting policy head outputs comparable action predictions. A learning-rate ablation confirms that encoder training matters far more than prior choice for policy performance, pointing to the pretrained encoder, not the prior, as the dominant factor. In short, action priors shape fine-tuning training dynamics, particularly in the observation embedding space, but do not affect policy performance. II Related Work II-A Flow-Matching and Diffusion Policies for Robotics Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become prominent approaches for visuomotor imitation learning. At their core, both families define time-dependent transport between a prior and target distribution in action space. Single-task diffusion policy [ 1 ] introduced the formulation, which was then extended in BESO [ 2 ] to goal-conditioned settings, and scaled in LBMs [ 14 , 4 , 3 , 5 ] . Compared to DDPM-based diffusion models [ 15 ] , flow-matching variants [ 6 ] take a more direct path from the prior to the target distribution and make no distributional assumption on the prior. These desirable properties are central to recent flow policies [ 5 , 4 ] and to this paper. Within the generative policy paradigm, LBMs (e.g., LBM 1.0 [ 3 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 4 ] , and GR00T N1.5 [ 5 ] ) pretrain on large-scale, diverse manipulation data before fine-tuning on downstream tasks, but by default use the Gaussian prior distribution in both pretraining and fine-tuning. Parallel empirical studies of fine-tuning design choices (action-space parameterization [ 16 ] , data scaling [ 17 ] , co-training [ 18 ] ) have examined many axes of the recipe but hold the prior fixed. Our paper investigates the effect of action prior choice on policy fine-tuning performance. II-B Pretraining, Transfer Learning, and Introspection Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model’s learned representations to new tasks, a form of transfer learning that has proven highly effective. Prior works have shown that pretrained features improve performance in both computer vision [ 19 , 20 ] and robotics: frozen pretrained encoders [ 21 , 22 ] , shared trunks [ 23 ] , and full pretrained policies [ 3 , 5 , 4 ] all outperform training from scratch. Other works examine what explains whether a pretrained model transfers well to a new task. Training-free probes such as LogME [ 24 ] estimate the predictive power of pretrained features. Scaling-law studies [ 25 , 26 ] and likelihood-based assessments [ 27 ] examine when pretraining metrics can be trusted as proxies for downstream policy performance. Our work applies these introspective tools to the choice of prior: we compare priors using downstream performance ( Section VI ) and training-free metrics, such as LogME, per-observation ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance, and cosine similarity in action and embedding spaces ( Section VII ). II-C Non-Gaussian Prior Distributions A growing body of work has proposed structured non-Gaussian priors for policy learning. BRIDGER [ 8 ] trains a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) to produce informative action priors. Cocos [ 9 ] uses a condition-dependent Gaussian whose parameters are learned from observations to prevent loss collapse. Retrieval [ 39 , 40 , 41 ] constructs the action prior from nearest-neighbor actions, with distances measured in the observation embedding space. Action-to-action flow matching [ 7 ] maps demonstration actions directly to target actions for single-step inference. Other variants include equivariance guarantees for non-Gaussian priors [ 10 ] , cluster-based and residual-action priors [ 28 , 29 ] , and Schrödinger-bridge formulations [ 30 , 31 ] . In each case, however, the proposed prior is evaluated by training a policy from scratch; none of these works investigates whether the benefit transfers to fine-tuning a pretrained LBM. A complementary line of research modifies the prior without changing the policy’s weights. Frozen-policy steering methods operate on the latent noise space of a trained policy: DSRL [ 32 ] defines a reward function over the noise space to denoise high-reward noise samples, Golden Ticket [ 33 ] searches for optimal constant noise vectors, and GoldenStart [ 34 ] trains a Q-guided CVAE noise prior. Related inference-time warm-starting methods [ 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 ] adjust the prior at rollout time. These methods change sampling, not training, and apply to any pretrained policy. Since we focus on the effects of training-time priors in fine-tuned policies, these approaches are outside the scope of this work. III Problem Setup Setting. We fine-tune a pretrained LBM π pre \pi_{\text{pre}} on task-specific demonstration datasets and consider whether replacing the default Gaussian prior with a non-Gaussian prior improves the fine-tuned policy performance. The pretrained policy π pre \pi_{\text{pre}} can be any flow-matching- or diffusion-based LBM (in our experiments: LBM 1.0 [ 3 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 4 ] , or GR00T N1.5 [ 5 ] ). Notation. We follow the diffusion policy notation [ 1 ] . The target a 1 a_{1} is an action chunk ( H H steps of future actions) drawn from the demonstration dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . The raw observation o o (camera images, language instructions, proprioception) is passed through the LBM’s vision-language-action encoder to produce the observation embedding e e , which conditions the action-head network v θ v_{\theta} . The action head is trained to transport prior samples a 0 ∼ p 0 a_{0}\sim p_{0} to targets a 1 a_{1} . We write a 0 ∼ p 0 a_{0}\sim p_{0} for a generic prior sample; the specific prior constructions (e.g., 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} , A pre A_{\text{pre}} , etc.) defined in Section IV each instantiate p 0 p_{0} . We use “prior” throughout the paper to refer to p 0 p_{0} . Why flow matching is the right testbed. Flow matching (FM) [ 6 ] regresses a velocity field directly between prior and target samples. The conditional FM objective ℒ FM \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}} = 𝔼 t , a 0 , a 1 ​ ‖ v θ ​ ( a t , t ∣ e ) − ( a 1 − a 0 ) ‖ 2 , \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t,a_{0},a_{1}}\left\|v_{\theta}(a_{t},t\mid e)-(a_{1}-a_{0})\right\|^{2}, (1) a t \displaystyle a_{t} = ( 1 − t ) ​ a 0 + t ​ a 1 , \displaystyle=(1-t)\,a_{0}+t\,a_{1}, only requires paired samples ( a 0 , a 1 ) (a_{0},a_{1}) from the prior and target, so swapping p 0 p_{0} from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) to any other distribution requires no change to the training or inference procedure. DDPM-style diffusion models [ 15 ] , by contrast, are designed around a forward noising process whose stationary distribution is Gaussian. Replacing this distribution would require redesigning the noise schedule, objective, and sampling procedure, which are non-trivial changes. We include three representative external priors effective for policy learning. • Cocos [ 9 ] is a condition-dependent Gaussian whose mean is produced by passing the observation embedding e e through a small encoder into the action space. The encoder is jointly trained with a decoder that maps back to the embedding space of e e . • BRIDGER [ 8 ] is a CVAE-based action prior that maps a Gaussian latent to an action chunk, conditioned on the observation embedding e e . • Retrieval ( k k -NN) [ 39 , 40 , 41 ] is a non-parametric prior that averages the k k nearest-neighbor action chunks from a frozen bank indexed by the observation embedding e e . The three cited works used k k -NN actions directly as policies; we repurpose this approach as a prior for fine-tuning. Some existing non-Gaussian prior methods, such as action-to-action FM [ 7 ] and VITA [ 42 ] , replace the policy network with a custom architecture, conflating the effect of the prior with architectural changes. These methods are thus incompatible with fine-tuning from pretrained weights. The seven priors above all preserve the pretrained encoder and action-head weights, so only the prior differs across experiments . V Experimental Setup In this section, we detail our experimental setup for evaluating whether and under what conditions non-Gaussian priors benefit policy fine-tuning. We cover: how we control for confounds, test for statistical significance, evaluate in simulation and on robot hardware, and define our plotting conventions. V-A Experimental Controls Throughout the paper, we hold the task, data, architecture, optimizer, and number of fine-tuning steps identical across all prior variants within each experimental setting (see Appendix C for hyperparameter choices). This protocol applies uniformly to all settings. For prior noise levels, we select σ A \sigma_{A} and σ E \sigma_{E} via grid search ( Fig. 19 ; values in Appendix A ). V-B Statistical Testing We treat policy comparison as a formal hypothesis test rather than only reporting empirical average success rates, following prior work [ 3 , 18 , 43 ] . For binary success/failure we use the STEP statistical framework [ 43 ] ; for continuous metrics (per-observation ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance and cosine similarity) we use Welch’s t t -test [ 44 ] . All tests use a global significance level α = 0.05 \alpha{=}0.05 (95% confidence level). When more than two priors are compared we apply Bonferroni correction: the family-wise false-positive probability of m m independent pairwise tests at level α \alpha is 1 − ( 1 − α ) m 1-(1-\alpha)^{m} . Bonferroni controls this by testing each pair at α / m \alpha/m such that the overall false-positive rate is upper-bounded by α \alpha . A compact letter display (CLD) [ 45 ] concisely summarizes each method comparison: two methods share at least one alphabetical letter if and only if their pairwise difference is not significant at the corrected level. Implementation details (STEP’s anytime-valid guarantee, Lai’s [ 46 ] fallback at per-method sample sizes above ∼ 600 {\sim}600 , and CLD ordering conventions) are in Appendix B . V-C Hardware A/B testing Following best practices for robot policy evaluation [ 47 ] , hardware rollouts use blind A/B testing: for each fixed initial condition (IC), all priors under evaluation are run in a randomized order before moving to the next IC, ensuring the human operator does not know which prior is being tested at any given trial. This design eliminates operator bias and, because priors are interleaved rather than grouped by prior, distributes any ambient drift (e.g., lighting, wear, operator attention) approximately equally across all priors. V-D Benchmarks We use two simulators and one hardware setup. The LBM Eval [ 3 ] Drake-based [ 48 ] simulation benchmark serves as our main testbed. It consists of eight bimanual manipulation tasks of varying difficulty and sample sizes (approximately 196–392 per task at 100%) that were unseen during the pretraining phase for LBM 1.0 (see [ 3 ] for pretraining data selection). We also evaluate on the RoboCasa365 [ 49 ] MuJoCo-based [ 50 ] simulation suite. This benchmark is split into 18 atomic tasks (single-step manipulations, e.g., opening a cabinet) and 16 composite tasks (multi-step sequences, e.g., preparing coffee), totaling 34 tasks. Hardware is a tabletop bimanual setup with two Franka FR3 arms and parallel grippers. Each rollout is scored by a human with a binary success label and a task-specific partial task progress rubric. The latter decomposes the task into ordered milestone predicates (e.g., rotor picked up , rotor seated , lockring tightened ) and reports the fraction of milestones achieved. Hardware details and per-task demonstration counts are in Appendix C . V-E Plotting Conventions In all figures, an ( ↑ \uparrow ) arrow indicates higher is better and a ( ↓ \downarrow ) arrow lower is better. Violin plots for binary success rates show Bayesian posterior distributions; a black horizontal tick marks the posterior mean and a colored dot marks the empirical mean. Violin plots for continuous metrics (e.g., ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance, cosine similarity, task progress) show empirical distributions with a colored dot at the empirical mean. All plots are annotated with CLD letters: methods sharing a letter are statistically indistinguishable; methods with different letters are statistically separable. LBM 1.0 [ 3 ] 20 225 VI Research Questions and Results Our experiments are guided by three research questions: (Q1) Do non-Gaussian priors that are measurably closer to the target improve policy fine-tuning performance? (Q2) Do informed priors have an advantage across data fractions, particularly in the low-data regime where the added inductive bias may be most beneficial? (Q3) Is the effect of prior choice consistent across model architectures as well as simulation and hardware experiments? We design four experimental settings, summarized in Table II , to carefully study these three questions. Setting A isolates Q1 using a contrived prior that is by construction closer in ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance to the target action distribution than the Gaussian. Setting B sim addresses both Q1 and Q2 by varying the amount of fine-tuning data across five fractions on eight tasks. Setting B real tests Q3 on whether the result transfers to hardware. Setting C further studies Q3 on other LBMs by repeating the experiments on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.5. We consistently find that non-Gaussian priors do not improve fine-tuning, with a possible exception in very low-data regimes. Alongside each main setting we run targeted ablations (encoder learning rate, training objective, noise scale), each isolating a single confounding variable. VI-A Setting A: Fraction-Pretrained Prior The key challenge in studying non-Gaussian priors for fine-tuning is controlling prior quality: a pretrained LBM has never seen the fine-tuning task, so its zero-shot actions may be out-of-distribution and form a weak prior. A null result would then be hard to tell apart from a poor-quality prior. Setting A therefore isolates this question by constructing an artificially strong prior that is measurably close to the target in ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance. We use a two-stage pipeline: first, the pretrained LBM 1.0 is fine-tuned using the Gaussian prior on 50% of the demonstrations to produce a task-aware checkpoint whose actions are much closer to the target than the Gaussian ( Fig. 2 , left); second, this checkpoint serves as the “pretrained model” for another round of fine-tuning, in which we vary only the prior. We evaluate on five kitchen-scenario tasks from LBM Eval (see Table VI for full names) and compare all seven priors from Table I , with 200 rollouts per task (1000 total per prior). Results. Fig. 3 summarizes the key finding across all seven prior variants. When training from scratch (i.e., training the same LBM 1.0 architecture from random weight initialization), all non-Gaussian priors (except for Cocos; see Appendix A ) outperform the Gaussian baseline 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} based on empirical success rates, though they are largely statistically indistinguishable. The simplest of our proposed priors, A pre A_{\text{pre}} , significantly outperforms 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} (CLD “a” vs. “bc”) with an average success rate of roughly 28% vs. 18%. This is consistent with prior work on non-Gaussian priors in the from-scratch regime [ 8 , 9 , 7 ] . Nevertheless, this empirical advantage disappears entirely in the fine-tuning regime: A pre A_{\text{pre}} becomes the worst-performing method based on success rate and no prior is statistically separable from the Gaussian. Additionally, the posterior distributions overlap more substantially in the fine-tuning case than in the from-scratch case, reflecting the lesser impact of action priors on policy performance during fine-tuning. VII Analysis: Why Does the Prior Not Matter Under Fine-Tuning? Summarizing the negative-result experiments against our research questions, we found that Q1 (closer priors should help) yields a negative answer, Q2 (advantage across fine-tuning data fractions) is only partly supported at 5% data, and Q3 (generalization across policies and hardware) also yields a negative answer. The experimental results thus raise a central question: if a non-Gaussian prior is measurably closer to the target distribution (in Setting A by construction, and in Settings B and C empirically), why does this proximity not translate to better fine-tuning performance? We approach this question from two complementary perspectives. First, we ask whether fine-tuned models converge toward the target despite starting from different priors. We examine convergence at two levels: whether different priors produce encoder features with comparable predictive power for the target actions ( Section VII-A ), and whether the resulting action predictions are similarly close to ground truth ( Section VII-B ). Second, we ask whether fine-tuned models diverge from a shared starting point : that is, whether different priors lead to structurally different optimization trajectories, as measured by ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance and cosine similarity in the action or embedding space ( Section VII-C ). The observed embedding-space divergence motivates a natural hypothesis: fine-tuning performance is governed primarily by the observation encoder rather than by the prior itself. We test this hypothesis directly through a learning-rate ablation that deliberately undertrains the encoder ( Section VII-D ). All analyses in this section are carried out in Setting B sim (LBM 1.0 simulation), where we have the most comprehensive results: seven prior variants × \times five data fractions × \times eight tasks, enabling controlled comparisons across the prior–data landscape. We focus on four representative priors: 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} (Gaussian), A pre A_{\text{pre}} (pure learned prior, closest to target), A pre + σ A ​ 𝒵 A_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{A}\mathcal{Z} (action + noise; defined in Section IV ), and E pre + σ E ​ 𝒵 E_{\text{pre}}{+}\sigma_{E}\mathcal{Z} (embedding + noise). The baselines (Cocos, BRIDGER, Retrieval) are omitted from these introspective ablations as their performance was found to be worse than or comparable to these four priors.
